claim: Coldcard, a security-obsessed air-gapped Bitcoin hardware wallet [made by Coinkite], was hacked [in an attack beginning July 30, 2026] [00:00]
quote: Coldcard, a security-obsessed air-gapped Bitcoin hardware wallet, was hacked
evidence: Coinkite's own July 30, 2026 advisory confirms a firmware flaw led to theft from affected devices; independently corroborated by TechCrunch and CBC coverage of the same event. [tier 1: Coinkite's own security advisory]

claim: Since July 30[, 2026], attackers have drained over 1,600 Bitcoin, worth about $100 million, from over 7,000 [Coldcard] wallets [00:00]
quote: attackers have drained over 1,600 Bitcoin, worth about $100 million, from over 7,000 wallets
evidence: Trackers disagree on the exact snapshot: TRM Labs put it at 1,816 BTC (~$116M) from 5,200+ addresses; crypto.news's 'confirmed losses' were 1,596 BTC (~$116M) across 4,585+ addresses with an estimated total of ~2,055 BTC (~$130M); Halborn cites ~7,300 affected addresses and $130M+. The video's figures sit inside this range on BTC and dollar value, but 'over 7,000 wallets' only matches the later, post-fourth-wave estimates rather than the contemporaneous count — a fast-moving, actively-updated on-chain figure at the time of publish, not a fixed one.

claim: The dollar losses from the Coldcard hack are only about half as much as they would have been if the same attack had happened a year earlier [00:00]
quote: it's only about half as much as they would have lost if the same thing happened a year ago
evidence: Yahoo Finance/Fortune: BTC was ≈$64,137 on Aug 5, 2026, 'roughly $50,000 lower... than the same time the previous year' (≈$114,000 on Aug 5, 2025). 64,137 / 114,000 ≈ 0.56 — the same stolen BTC amount would be worth about 56% today of what it was worth a year ago, close to 'about half.'

claim: The attackers pulled off the Coldcard hack without any malware, phishing, or physical coercion [00:00]
quote: they pulled it off without any malware, phishing, or lead pipes
evidence: All independent writeups describe a purely computational, remote brute-force attack against weak on-device entropy — deriving private keys offline and checking them against the public blockchain, with no malware or phishing of victims involved.

claim: A properly generated [BIP39, 12-word] seed phrase has 128 bits of entropy [01:03]
quote: A properly generated seed phrase has 128 bits of entropy
evidence: Coinkite's own advisory states unaffected devices produce seeds with 'the expected 128 bits' of entropy — the standard for a 12-word BIP39 mnemonic.

claim: [Given 128 bits of entropy, claim 5,] trying a billion guesses per second [to brute-force a seed phrase] would take far longer than the age of the universe [01:03]
quote: if you try a billion guesses per second, the universe would end before you got close
evidence: 2^128 ≈ 3.40×10^38 possible keys ÷ 1e9 guesses/sec ≈ 3.40×10^29 seconds ≈ 7.8×10^11 times the current age of the universe (≈4.35×10^17 s, i.e. 13.8By). Arithmetic checks out on the true 128-bit input from claim 5 — this verifies the calculator, not a separate fact about the world.

claim: Coldcard is made by [the] Canadian company Coinkite [01:03]
quote: made by Canadian company Coinkite
evidence: Coinkite Inc. is based in Toronto, Canada, and makes Coldcard and related hardware there — confirmed on Coldcard's own about page and in CBC's coverage of the hack.

claim: For [five] years [before the July 2026 hack], the Coldcard [device] never [used its own onboard hardware random number generator, without Coinkite knowing] [01:03]
quote: for the last 5 years, without them knowing, the Coldcard never did
evidence: The bug was introduced with the March 2021 libsecp256k1/libNgU migration and was discovered/disclosed July 30, 2026 — about five years, matching the 'five-year-old firmware flaw' framing used across coverage.

claim: The Coldcard's firmware runs on MicroPython, which ships its own basic random number generator [02:06]
quote: The Coldcard's firmware runs on MicroPython, which ships its own basic random number generator
evidence: Confirmed: MicroPython's built-in PRNG (Yasmarang) is the software fallback that silently ended up generating seeds instead of Coldcard's hardware TRNG.

claim: Coinkite's own hardware RNG and MicroPython's software RNG exposed a function with the exact same name, and because a disabling flag was technically defined (set to zero) rather than undefined, an 'if not defined' check in the crypto library passed and every Coldcard seed phrase was generated by MicroPython's basic RNG instead of Coinkite's hardware RNG [02:06]
quote: both number generators exposed a function with the exact same name… because the flag was technically defined just as a zero, the check passed
evidence: Coinkite's own advisory: the MICROPY_HW_ENABLE_RNG=0 flag was meant to disable the software RNG, but the library's check 'asked whether the flag was defined… not whether it was enabled... the flag was defined with a value of zero... the check only asked does this exist? and the answer was yes' — so libNgU's rng_get() symbol resolved to MicroPython's Yasmarang implementation. Near word-for-word match to the video's account. [tier 1: Coinkite's own advisory]

claim: [Coldcard's fallback] random number generator faked randomness using the chip's serial number and a timer, both of which are deterministic [02:06]
quote: it fakes it using the chip's serial number and a timer, both of which are deterministic
evidence: Technical writeup: the fallback PRNG 'was initialized from the chip's unique serial number and timer registers, collecting no fresh entropy afterward' — both deterministic and estimable by an attacker, matching the video's description.

claim: In under an hour[, on July 30, 2026], the first attacker drained over 1,000 Bitcoin from nearly 1,200 [Coldcard] addresses [02:06]
quote: In under an hour, the first attacker drained over 1,000 Bitcoin from nearly 1,200 addresses
evidence: TechCrunch/CBC: the attacker drained 1,196 addresses in 41 minutes on July 30, taking 1,082.65 BTC (~$70.2M at the time) — matches 'under an hour... over 1,000 Bitcoin from nearly 1,200 addresses' closely.

claim: The [first Coldcard hack] attacker hit the biggest wallets first [02:06]
quote: hitting the biggest wallets first
evidence: Chainalysis's on-chain analysis (reported by CryptoTimes) found the attacker hit high-value wallets early, pulling roughly $30M in the first 10 minutes — deliberate targeting of the largest balances, not random or generation order.

claim: After two more attacks over the [July 30] weekend, the [Coldcard hack] total reached nearly 1,800 Bitcoin from over 7,000 addresses [03:09]
quote: nearly 1,800 Bitcoin from over 7,000 addresses
evidence: TRM Labs' running total (as of ~Aug 3) was 1,816 BTC (~$116M) from 'more than 5,200 addresses' — matches 'nearly 1,800 Bitcoin' well but falls short of 'over 7,000 addresses' at that point. Halborn's ~7,300-address figure appears to already fold in the Monday fourth wave, which the video narrates separately in the next beat — the address count likely anticipates a wave the story hasn't reached yet.

claim: [Coinkite's] CEO apologized and took full accountability [for the Coldcard bug] [03:09]
quote: The Coinkite CEO apologized and took full accountability
evidence: Coinkite CEO Rodolfo Novak publicly apologized on X (July 31), calling the company 'heartbroken' and accepting 'full accountability for the firmware bug.'

claim: Because Bitcoin has no way to rotate a [compromised private] key, the only way for [Coldcard hack] victims to recover was to generate a brand new seed and move their coins with an on-chain transaction [03:09]
quote: Because Bitcoin has no way to rotate a key, the only way out is for victims to generate a brand new seed and move their coins with an actual on-chain transaction
evidence: Coinkite's advisory: fixed firmware was released (4.2.0+ etc.), but 'updating the firmware does not change or repair an existing seed' — affected users must move funds to a freshly generated seed, exactly as described. Bitcoin itself has no key-rotation primitive.

claim: [In the Coldcard hack,] every [Bitcoin] transaction waits in the public mempool until a miner includes it in a block, so the attacker could watch the mempool for transactions from a compromised address and outbid the victim's rescue transaction with a higher fee, since miners confirm the highest-fee transaction first [03:09]
quote: the attacker can just watch the mempool for anything coming from a compromised address
evidence: Multiple outlets: attackers 'monitored the public mempool and submitted competing transactions with higher fees to drain wallets before victims' rescue transactions confirmed' — standard Bitcoin fee-priority mechanics, matching the video.

claim: When a fourth [Coldcard hack] attack went live on [the] Monday morning [after July 30, 2026], the only way [for victims] to win was to send the rescue transaction directly to a mining pool, bypassing the public mempool [03:09]
quote: the only way to win was to skip the public mempool entirely and send your rescue transaction directly to a mining pool since the bot can't outbid a transaction it never sees
evidence: MARA's Slipstream service let victims send rescue transactions 'straight to its mining pool instead of broadcasting them to the public network,' keeping the transaction hidden until mined so attacker bots couldn't see and outbid it — matches the video's description of the workaround.

claim: Every unsold Coldcard device in Coinkite's warehouse carried the same broken firmware, so Coinkite had to hold shipments and pull the remaining inventory from sale [04:11]
quote: hold shipments and take the remaining inventory out to the pasture
evidence: Coverage of Coinkite's response: the company 'destroyed remaining inventory manufactured with the vulnerable firmware, and shipment was halted' — consistent with, if more drastic than, the video's 'hold shipments... take the remaining inventory out to the pasture.'

quote: Over 50 million projects have already been built with Lovable
